choices.text: Sensitivity and specificity stay at 0.80 and 0.90, but PPV collapses
choices.feedback: Exactly. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test. PPV and NPV depend on how many diseased people are in the pool being tested.

choices.text: Sensitivity falls because the test performs worse in healthy people
choices.feedback: Sensitivity is measured only among diseased patients, so the size of the healthy group cannot change it. What changes is the mix of positives.

choices.text: Nothing changes, the test is the test
choices.feedback: Half right. The test characteristics hold, but predictive values are not test characteristics. That distinction is the whole point of this problem.

steps.prompt: Compute it out of 100,000 screened at 0.1 percent prevalence: 100 have cancer, 99,900 do not. Work through the new PPV.

choices.text: True positives 80, false positives 9,990, so PPV = 80 / 10,070 = 0.008
choices.feedback: Correct arithmetic: 0.80 x 100 = 80 true positives, and 10 percent of 99,900 = 9,990 false positives. Under 1 percent of positives are real cancers.

choices.text: PPV stays near 0.47 because the test has not changed
choices.feedback: The test has not changed but the population has. The 99,900 healthy people generate almost 10,000 false alarms, drowning the 80 true cases.

choices.text: PPV = 80 / 100 = 0.80 because 80 of the cancers were found
choices.feedback: That is sensitivity once more. The denominator for PPV is always everyone who tested positive, including the false alarms.

choices.text: Roughly 1 in 125 positives is a true cancer
choices.feedback: Same answer stated as odds: 80 out of 10,070 is about 1 in 126. Correct reasoning, and a useful way to explain it to a patient.

steps.prompt: Final question: what recommendation follows from a PPV of 0.8 percent in the general population?

choices.text: Do not use it for population screening; reserve it for high-risk groups where prevalence supports the result
choices.feedback: Right, and this is why screening guidelines are written around prevalence, not around test accuracy alone. Nearly 10,000 people would face workup for nothing.

choices.text: Screen everyone, since 80 cancers would be caught early
choices.feedback: Those 80 are real, but weigh them against 9,990 false alarms, each meaning imaging, biopsy risk and months of fear. That is the harm side of screening.

choices.text: Raise the positivity threshold to gain specificity, then re-evaluate
choices.feedback: A defensible engineering answer. More specificity cuts false positives, but it costs sensitivity, and at this prevalence even 99 percent specificity leaves about 1,000 false alarms.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to carry out of this problem: sensitivity and specificity describe the test, predictive values describe the test plus the population. Whenever a question gives you a prevalence, it is telling you the answer will hinge on it. Build the 2x2 table out of a round number of people, fill in all four cells, and read every quantity as one cell divided by one margin. Sensitivity divides by the disease column, PPV divides by the positive row. Those two denominators are the entire difference, and confusing them is the single most common error in clinical probability.

scenarios.title: Problem set: choosing and running the right test
scenarios.intro: Second problem on the board. A trial randomizes 60 patients with hypertension to a new drug or placebo, 30 per arm, and measures systolic blood pressure after 8 weeks. Drug arm: mean 132.0 mmHg, sd 12.0. Placebo arm: mean 140.0 mmHg, sd 14.0. You must pick a test, run it, and state what the p-value does and does not say.

steps.prompt: Two independent groups, one quantitative outcome, roughly symmetric data. Which analysis?

choices.text: Independent two-sample t-test
choices.feedback: Correct. Two separate groups of different people, a continuous outcome, and no pairing between them. That is the textbook two-sample t-test.

choices.text: Paired t-test on the two arms
choices.feedback: Pairing requires a link between a specific drug patient and a specific placebo patient. These are separate randomized people, so there is nothing to pair.

choices.text: Chi-square test of independence
choices.feedback: Chi-square compares counts in categories. Blood pressure is quantitative, so a chi-square would throw away most of the information.

choices.text: One-way ANOVA with two groups
choices.feedback: Not wrong, actually. With exactly two groups ANOVA gives the same p-value as the t-test, since F equals t squared. The t-test is the conventional report.

steps.prompt: State the hypotheses before touching a calculator.

choices.text: H0: mu1 = mu2. Ha: mu1 is not equal to mu2, two-tailed
choices.feedback: Right. The null is always no difference, and a two-tailed alternative is the honest default unless the protocol pre-specified a direction.

choices.text: H0: the drug lowers pressure. Ha: the drug does nothing
choices.feedback: Reversed. The null must be the no-effect claim, because the whole procedure computes probabilities assuming the null is true.

choices.text: H0: xbar1 = xbar2
choices.feedback: Hypotheses are about population parameters (mu), never about the sample means you observed. Those are already known and clearly unequal.

steps.prompt: Compute the standard error of the difference. The pooled version is SE = sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2) with s1 = 12, s2 = 14, n1 = n2 = 30.

choices.feedback: Correct all the way through: square each sd, divide by its n, add, then take the root. 3.37 mmHg is the noise level of the difference.
Numerically close by accident, but the method is wrong. Standard deviations are never averaged directly; variances add, standard deviations do not.

choices.text: SE = 12 / sqrt(30) = 2.19 mmHg
choices.feedback: That is the standard error of the drug arm alone. A comparison needs the uncertainty of both arms combined.

steps.prompt: The observed difference is 140.0 - 132.0 = 8.0 mmHg and SE = 3.37. Compute t and compare it to the critical value of about 2.00 at df near 58.

choices.text: t = 8.0 / 3.37 = 2.37, which exceeds 2.00, so reject H0
choices.feedback: Correct. The difference is 2.37 standard errors from zero, past the 5 percent threshold. The two-tailed p-value is about 0.021.

choices.text: t = 8.0, which is obviously large, so reject H0
choices.feedback: That is the raw difference in mmHg, not a test statistic. A difference only becomes evidence once scaled by how noisy it is.

choices.text: t = 8.0 / 12 = 0.67, so fail to reject H0
choices.feedback: Dividing by a standard deviation rather than the standard error of the difference. That mistake almost always produces a false negative.

steps.prompt: The paper will report p = 0.021. A classmate says that means there is a 2.1 percent chance the drug does not work. Respond.

choices.text: Wrong direction: p is the probability of seeing a difference this large or larger IF the drug truly did nothing
choices.feedback: Exactly right. The p-value is conditional on the null being true; it never gives the probability that a hypothesis is true.

choices.text: Close enough, since 1 - p is the probability the drug works
choices.feedback: That is the same error restated. Assigning probability to a hypothesis requires a prior and Bayesian machinery, which a p-value does not contain.

choices.text: It also means the effect is large, since p is small
choices.feedback: A small p can come from a tiny effect measured in a huge sample. Significance and magnitude are separate questions.

choices.text: Better to report the difference of 8.0 mmHg with its 95 percent CI, roughly 1.3 to 14.7 mmHg
choices.feedback: The best answer of all: 8.0 plus or minus 2.00 x 3.37 gives that interval, which conveys both significance and the plausible size of the benefit.

steps.prompt: Last call. The lower bound of the CI is about 1.3 mmHg. What does the trial actually support?

choices.text: A real average reduction, but the data are compatible with a benefit as small as roughly 1 mmHg
choices.feedback: Correct and appropriately cautious. The interval excludes zero, so the effect is real, yet its lower end may be clinically trivial.

choices.text: The drug reliably lowers systolic pressure by 8 mmHg in every patient
choices.feedback: The 8 mmHg is an average of group means, not a promise for an individual, and the interval shows considerable uncertainty even about the average.

choices.text: Nothing, because 60 patients is too few to conclude anything
choices.feedback: Too dismissive. The test accounted for the sample size; small n widens the interval rather than invalidating the result.

scenarios.debrief: Three habits to take from this walkthrough. First, choose the test from the design: count the groups, ask whether they are independent or paired, and check whether the outcome is quantitative or categorical. Two independent groups with a quantitative outcome means a two-sample t-test every time. Second, a test statistic is always an observed difference divided by its standard error, and standard errors of a difference come from adding variances, never from averaging standard deviations. Third, the p-value answers only one question, how surprising the data would be under the null, so pair it with the effect size and its confidence interval. A result can be statistically significant and clinically minor, and the interval is what tells you which.
